title: Magnetic materials: the magnet that sorts metals, even the ones it does not attract

summary.text: A magnet ignores an aluminium can lying on a table, because aluminium is not a magnetic material. Yet if you swish a strong magnet quickly past the can, the can rolls after it. Your child maps which parts of kitchen steel stick to a magnet, makes a can follow a magnet, and swings a magnet over four plates to see which one stops it. Then they see how a recycling centre sorts a heap of scrap by using both facts, and why an induction stove only heats some pans.
summary.art: An aluminium cold-drink can lying on a table rolling towards a strong magnet that is being swished past it, with a plastic bottle beside it that does not move.

intro.hook: Hold a magnet against an aluminium cold-drink can. Nothing happens, because aluminium is not magnetic. Now lay the can on its side and swish a strong magnet quickly past it, without touching. The can rolls after the magnet. If the can is not magnetic, what is pushing it?
intro.text: In Class 3 you found out that a magnet attracts iron, nickel and cobalt, and that most other materials seem to ignore it. This unit goes one step deeper. You find out that the word 'ignore' was only true for a magnet that sits still. You also look closely at steel, which is not one material but a family, and at how a scrap yard or a recycling centre uses these facts to sort metal at high speed.
intro.art: A hand swishing a silver magnet past an aluminium can on a wooden table, with the can starting to roll after it.

outcomes: I can explain that materials answer a magnet in three ways: strong attraction, very weak attraction and very weak repulsion.
I can map which parts of a steel thing a magnet sticks to, and say why two steel things can answer differently.
I can show that a moving magnet pushes on a metal such as aluminium or copper, even though a still magnet ignores it.
I can explain, in simple words, that this push comes from swirling electric currents in the metal, called eddy currents.
I can say which materials show this push most, and why plastic, wood and glass do not.
I can describe how a recycling centre sorts scrap with a magnet, an eddy current separator and other steps.
I can explain why a pan must have a magnetic base to work on an induction stove.
I can say what a magnet test can and cannot tell us about a material, and why 'magnetic' depends on how we test.

terms.meaning: A material that a still magnet attracts strongly, such as iron, nickel and cobalt. The word comes from the Latin for iron.
terms.example: A steel nail is made of a ferromagnetic material.
terms.art: A steel nail clinging to a magnet.

terms.meaning: A material that is attracted extremely weakly by a very strong magnet, so weakly that we cannot feel it. Aluminium is one.
terms.example: Aluminium is paramagnetic. A fridge magnet does not move it at all.
terms.art: A strong magnet and a tiny arrow pointing from an aluminium block towards it.

terms.meaning: A material that is pushed away extremely weakly by a very strong magnet. Most materials are, including water, wood, copper and gold.
terms.example: A strong lab magnet can lift a drop of water, because water is diamagnetic.
terms.art: A drop of water floating above a strong magnet.

terms.meaning: A swirl of electric current that a moving magnet makes inside a piece of metal. An eddy is a small whirl, like the one at the edge of a river.
terms.example: A moving magnet makes eddy currents in an aluminium can.
terms.art: Curved arrows swirling in a flat metal plate under a moving magnet.

terms.meaning: Making an electric current by moving a magnet near a conductor, or by changing a magnetic field. Michael Faraday found it in 1831.
terms.example: A bicycle dynamo lights a lamp by induction.
terms.art: A magnet being moved in and out of a coil of wire with a small bulb lighting.

terms.meaning: A material that electricity passes through easily. Metals are conductors. The best are silver, copper, gold and aluminium.
terms.example: Copper is used in wires because it conducts well.
terms.art: A coil of copper wire beside a plastic-coated cable.

terms.meaning: A material that electricity does not pass through. Plastic, wood, glass and rubber are insulators.
terms.example: The plastic around a wire is an insulator.
terms.art: A wire with a plastic coating, with an electricity arrow stopped at the plastic.

terms.meaning: A metal that has iron in it, such as steel. A magnet usually attracts a ferrous metal.
terms.example: Steel and cast iron are ferrous metals.
terms.art: A steel spoon and an iron tawa side by side.

terms.meaning: A metal with no iron in it, such as aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver. A still magnet does not attract it.
terms.example: Aluminium, copper and brass are non-ferrous metals.
terms.art: An aluminium can, a copper pot and a brass diya in a row.

terms.meaning: Steel with chromium mixed in, so that it hardly rusts. There are many kinds. Some stick to a magnet and some do not.
terms.example: Many tumblers are stainless steel. Many induction pans are too.
terms.art: A steel tumbler and a steel pan base with a magnet touching each.

terms.meaning: A mixture of a metal with other metals or substances, made to do a job better.
terms.example: Brass is copper mixed with zinc. Steel is iron mixed with a little carbon.
terms.art: Two small heaps of copper and zinc flowing into a brass bell.

terms.meaning: Bending, rolling or hammering a piece of metal without heating it. It can change the metal inside, and sometimes its magnetism.
terms.example: The bent neck of a steel spoon can stick to a magnet a little more than its smooth bowl.
terms.art: A steel spoon being bent in a vice.

terms.meaning: A cooker that heats a pan using a changing magnetic field, with no flame and no red-hot ring.
terms.example: A steel pan with a magnetic base works on an induction stove. An aluminium pan usually does not.
terms.art: A flat glass cooker top with a steel pan on it.

terms.meaning: A strong magnet over a conveyor belt, which lifts out the iron and steel from mixed waste.
terms.example: A recycling centre uses a magnetic separator to take steel cans out of a stream of mixed waste.
terms.art: A big magnet above a conveyor belt lifting steel cans out of a heap.

terms.meaning: A machine with a fast-spinning drum of magnets, which throws aluminium and other non-ferrous metals off a conveyor belt.
terms.example: At a recycling centre, an eddy current separator flings aluminium cans into one bin while plastic falls into another.
terms.art: A conveyor belt ending in a spinning magnetic drum, with cans leaping forward into a bin.

terms.meaning: A device with a coil that makes a changing magnetic field. It finds metal, even non-magnetic metal, by sensing the eddy currents the metal makes.
terms.example: The metal detector arch at an airport finds a metal key, whether or not the key is magnetic.
terms.art: A person walking through a metal detector arch while a coil in the arch glows.

terms.meaning: The brown flaky mixture of iron and oxygen that forms when iron or steel stays damp. Iron in rust is joined with oxygen.
terms.example: A nail left in a wet place for weeks is covered in rust.
terms.art: A rusty nail beside a clean new nail.

terms.meaning: Collecting used materials and turning them into new things. Metals can be melted and made into new metal again and again.
terms.example: Aluminium cans can be melted and made into new cans.
terms.art: A heap of crushed cans and a stack of new shiny cans.

explanations.concept: Three ways a material answers a magnet
explanations.definition: A material can be strongly attracted by a magnet, which is called ferromagnetic. It can be attracted extremely weakly, which is called paramagnetic. Or it can be pushed away extremely weakly, which is called diamagnetic.
explanations.description: At home you sort materials into two boxes, 'sticks' and 'does not stick'. Scientists find three kinds of answer. Iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly attracted, and we feel it. Aluminium, platinum, magnesium and the oxygen in the air are attracted so weakly that only a very sensitive machine notices. Copper, gold, silver, water, wood and most other things are pushed away just as weakly. In 1845, Michael Faraday used the words paramagnetic and diamagnetic to tell the two weak kinds apart. A fridge magnet cannot show the weak answers. A huge magnet in a laboratory can.
examples: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic, and a still magnet clings to them.
Aluminium and the oxygen in air are paramagnetic, and are pulled a tiny bit.
Water, copper, gold, wood and your hand are diamagnetic, and are pushed away a tiny bit.
explanations.art: Three columns labelled strong pull, very weak pull and very weak push, with an iron nail, an aluminium block and a drop of water below them.

explanations.concept: A still magnet ignores aluminium. A moving magnet does not.
explanations.definition: A magnet that is moving past a piece of aluminium or copper makes the metal push against it, even though the same magnet held still does nothing.
explanations.description: Lay an aluminium can on its side and hold a strong magnet still beside it. Nothing happens. Now swish the magnet quickly past the can. The can rolls after the magnet. If you pass the magnet over an aluminium plate, you feel a drag, as if the magnet were moving through thick honey. Slow down, and the drag fades. Stop, and it is gone. So what a material does depends on what the magnet is doing, as well as on what the material is made of. This push is not the attraction that a magnet has for iron. It comes from electricity: the moving magnet makes electric currents swirl inside the metal.
examples: A strong magnet swished past an aluminium can makes the can roll after it.
A magnet dropped through a thick copper pipe falls much more slowly than through a plastic pipe.
A magnet pulled quickly across an aluminium plate feels a drag.
explanations.art: A magnet moving past an aluminium can on a table with a small arrow showing the can following.

explanations.concept: Eddy currents: swirls of electricity in metal
explanations.definition: A moving magnet makes electric currents in any piece of metal that carries electricity. In a solid plate or can, these currents swirl round in loops, and are called eddy currents.
explanations.description: In 1831, Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet in and out of a coil of wire makes electricity flow in the wire. This is called induction. A flat plate of metal is like a coil with a huge number of loops, in every direction. When a magnet moves near it, electricity swirls round inside the plate. 'Eddy' means a small whirl, like the one you see in a river behind a rock. In 1855, the French scientist Leon Foucault found that a copper disc spinning between the poles of a strong magnet gets hot. The swirling electricity heats the metal as it flows. The same effect is used in induction stoves.
examples: The eddy currents in a moving aluminium can are made by the magnet that moves past it.
Foucault's copper disc became hot when it was spun between the poles of a magnet.
A bicycle dynamo lights a lamp because a moving magnet makes electricity in a coil.
explanations.art: A flat metal plate with a magnet moving above it and curved arrows swirling inside the plate.

explanations.concept: The swirls push back: why the can follows
explanations.definition: Eddy currents make a magnetic field of their own. It always pushes against the change that made it. So the metal is dragged along by the moving magnet, and the magnet is slowed by the metal.
explanations.description: The swirling current in the can is an electric current, and every electric current makes a magnetic field. That new field acts on the moving magnet. In 1834, the physicist Heinrich Lenz showed that it always works against the movement that made it. A magnet swishing past a can is pushed back by the can's field, and the can is pulled forward by the magnet's field. These two pushes are equal and opposite, as every push and pull is. That is why the can rolls after the magnet. The same thing makes a magnet fall slowly through a copper pipe. The pipe's swirls push up against the falling magnet. When the magnet stops moving, the swirls fade away, and the push is gone.
examples: A can follows a fast-moving magnet, and a slow magnet hardly moves it.
A magnet swinging over an aluminium plate slows down and stops in a few swings.
A magnet falls slowly in a thick copper pipe, because the pipe pushes up on it.
explanations.art: A magnet falling through a copper pipe with swirl arrows in the pipe and an upward arrow on the magnet.

explanations.concept: Why good conductors show it most
explanations.definition: The stronger the eddy currents, the stronger the push. Eddy currents are strongest in metals that carry electricity very well and in thick pieces.
explanations.description: Silver, copper, gold and aluminium carry electricity better than other metals. Swirls flow easily in them, so a magnet moving near them feels a strong drag. Steel and stainless steel carry electricity less well, so the effect is weaker. Brass is in the middle. Plastic, wood, glass and rubber do not carry electricity at all, so a moving magnet feels nothing. A thick piece gives more room for swirls than a thin one. If you cut slits in a metal plate, the swirls cannot flow round and the drag falls. So the drag depends on the material, the shape of the piece and the speed of the magnet.
examples: A thick aluminium plate drags a swinging magnet to a stop much sooner than a thin foil.
A wooden or plastic board does not drag a magnet at all.
A copper pipe slows a falling magnet more than a stainless steel pipe does.
explanations.art: Two metal plates, one solid with big swirls and one with slits and tiny swirls.

explanations.concept: How a recycling centre sorts metal
explanations.definition: A recycling centre takes iron and steel out of a stream of mixed waste with a magnet. Then it throws out aluminium and other non-ferrous metals with an eddy current separator.
explanations.description: Mixed waste rides on a conveyor belt. A strong magnet hangs over the belt and lifts out steel cans, nails and lids, because steel is ferromagnetic. The rest rides on to the end of the belt, where a drum of magnets spins very fast inside the belt roller. Aluminium cans are not attracted to magnets. But the quickly changing magnetic field makes eddy currents in them, and these push the cans forward, so they jump off the end of the belt. Plastic and glass fall straight down. So a single belt can sort the waste into three heaps. Blowers, sieves, cameras and human hands do the rest. In India, much of this sorting is done by waste pickers and kabadiwalas. They use their eyes, their hands, the sound a piece makes when it is tapped and, sometimes, a magnet.
examples: A strong magnet hanging over a conveyor belt lifts steel cans off the belt in a recycling centre.
An eddy current separator makes aluminium cans leap off the end of a belt.
A waste picker taps a vessel and listens to the ring to tell brass from steel.
explanations.art: A conveyor belt with a big magnet above lifting steel cans, and a spinning drum at the end throwing aluminium cans into a separate bin.

explanations.concept: Why an induction stove needs a magnetic pan
explanations.definition: An induction stove makes a fast-changing magnetic field. In a steel pan with a magnetic base, this field makes strong eddy currents that heat the pan itself. A pan that a magnet does not stick to usually heats badly or not at all.
explanations.description: There is no flame and no red-hot coil in an induction stove. Under the glass there is a flat coil of wire with a fast-changing electric current in it. It makes a fast-changing magnetic field above the glass. When a pan with a base of magnetic steel sits there, the field makes eddy currents in the base. It also keeps flipping the tiny magnets inside the steel back and forth. Both heat the steel, and the steel heats the food. The glass stays cool, apart from heat coming back from the pan. An aluminium pan carries electricity so well that the eddy currents heat it very little. It is also not magnetic. So a pan for an induction stove must have a magnetic steel base. A simple test is to put a magnet on the base. If it sticks firmly, the pan will probably work.
examples: A pan with a base that holds a fridge magnet firmly will usually work on an induction stove.
An aluminium cooker usually does not work unless it has a steel disc in its base.
Cast iron and many stainless steel pans work well on induction.
explanations.art: A glass induction cooker top with a coil drawn under it, a steel pan above and curved field lines passing into the pan.

explanations.concept: Same steel, different answers: bending can change magnetism
explanations.definition: Stainless steel is a family of mixtures. Some kinds stick to a magnet strongly, some hardly at all. A kind that hardly sticks can stick a little more where it has been bent, rolled or hammered.
explanations.description: The common stainless steel of tumblers and katoris has chromium and nickel in it. The nickel keeps the iron atoms packed in a pattern in which the tiny magnets of the iron atoms do not line up, so a magnet hardly attracts it. But if you bend or roll this steel, some of its atoms are pushed into another pattern, and there the tiny magnets can line up. That is why a magnet may stick slightly to the rim of a tumbler, the bent neck of a spoon or the folded edge of a sink, but not to the flat wall. Other stainless steels, with less nickel, stick all over, and pans for induction stoves are made from those. Because the mixture and the shaping both matter, you cannot tell which kind of steel a thing is made of by its shine. You have to test the place you care about.
examples: A magnet may cling weakly to the rolled rim of a steel tumbler but not to its smooth wall.
A steel spoon may stick a little at the bent neck and not at the bowl.
A pan sold for induction cooking is made so that a magnet sticks firmly to its base.
explanations.art: A steel tumbler with small dots at the rim and base showing where a magnet sticks, and none on the smooth wall.

explanations.concept: Metal detectors find metal that is not magnetic
explanations.definition: A metal detector makes a changing magnetic field, which makes eddy currents in nearby metal. The detector senses the field of those currents. So it finds gold, silver, copper and aluminium, even though magnets do not attract them.
explanations.description: A metal detector's search coil has a changing current in it. That makes a changing magnetic field around the coil. If a coin, a key or a ring is near the coil, the field makes eddy currents in it. The eddy currents make a small magnetic field of their own, which the coil can sense. The detector beeps. No attraction is needed. The airport arch you walk through uses the same idea. A magnet alone would find only iron things. A metal detector finds any metal that carries electricity. Salt water and wet soil also carry electricity, so they can confuse the machine.
examples: A metal detector at an airport finds a brass key and a gold ring.
A hobbyist with a search coil finds old coins in a field.
A magnet alone cannot find a coin made of copper.
explanations.art: A hand holding a metal detector over a coin buried in sand, with field lines and swirl arrows in the coin.

explanations.concept: What the magnet sees in rust
explanations.definition: Rust is not one substance. It is a mixture of iron joined with oxygen and water. Some forms of it are magnetic and some are almost not.
explanations.description: When iron stays damp, it slowly changes into rust. The brown flaky outside of a rusty nail is mostly iron joined with oxygen and water, in forms that are only weakly magnetic. But a rusty nail still has a core of iron under the flakes, so a magnet still sticks to the nail. Some forms of iron joined with oxygen, such as the black magnetite of lodestone, are strongly magnetic. Rust flakes that have fallen off may stick faintly, or not at all. A magnet is a good tool for finding iron that is still iron. It is a poor tool for finding iron that has turned into rust. So a magnet still sticks to a rusty bridge, because of the iron under the rust, but it hardly sticks to the rust itself.
examples: A rusty nail still sticks to a magnet because its core is still iron.
Brown rust flakes on a plate usually stick faintly or not at all.
Black magnetite sand sticks strongly to a magnet.
explanations.art: A rusty nail with a cut-away showing a grey iron core under brown flaky rust.

explanations.concept: Magnets on Mars: iron in red dust
explanations.definition: Mars is red because its dust is rich in iron joined with oxygen. Landers and rovers on Mars have carried magnets, and the dust that clings to them shows that some of it has magnetic iron minerals.
explanations.description: Much of the soil in India is red for the same reason that Mars is red. Red laterite soil, for example in Kerala and Karnataka, gets its colour from iron oxide, which is iron joined with oxygen. The dust on Mars is coloured by iron in the same way. The Viking landers of 1976 and later rovers carried small magnets, and the dust that clung to them showed that a part of it is magnetic. This means that even on another planet, a plain magnet and a spoonful of dust can tell us something about the rocks. Scientists think that some of the iron minerals formed when the planet had water. Others may have formed in different ways. The details are still being worked out.
examples: Red laterite soil in Kerala and Karnataka is coloured by iron oxide.
A magnet on a Mars rover collects magnetic dust.
Red brick is red because of iron in the clay.
explanations.art: A rover on a red plain with a small magnet on its arm covered with dark dust.

explanations.concept: Is 'magnetic' something a material has, or something we find by testing?
explanations.description: In school we say 'iron is magnetic and aluminium is not.' But aluminium answers a still magnet with almost nothing, and a moving magnet with a clear push. So is 'magnetic' a label for the material, or for how the material answers one kind of test? Scientists and thinkers do not all say the same.
examples: Iron is attracted by a still magnet, and aluminium is not, but aluminium is dragged by a moving one.
A stainless steel tumbler may stick at the rim and not on the wall.
Iron stops being magnetic when it is red hot, and is magnetic again when it cools.

perspectives.explanation: Magnetic behaviour comes from the way the electrons are arranged in the atoms of a material. This arrangement is a fact about the material, so 'ferromagnetic' is a real property. The moving magnet effect is a different thing, which belongs to electricity.

What matters is what the material does in the job. A pan is 'magnetic' enough if it works on an induction stove. A scrap dealer labels a heap by what a still magnet and a moving magnet do to it. So the label belongs to the test.
He said that a road is made by walking on it, and things are so because we call them so. Labels are made by people. They are useful, but they are not the whole of the thing.

explanations.art: An aluminium can answering a still magnet with a blank bubble and a moving magnet with a rolling arrow.

agreed.text: At room temperature, a still magnet strongly attracts only iron, nickel, cobalt and some mixtures of them.
agreed.evidence: Thousands of materials have been tested. Everyone who tests kitchen things with a magnet finds the same.

agreed.text: A moving magnet makes swirling electric currents in any piece of metal that carries electricity.
agreed.evidence: Faraday showed it in 1831. Foucault found in 1855 that a copper disc spun between magnet poles gets hot.

agreed.text: The swirling currents push against the magnet's motion, which slows a falling magnet and drags a metal can along.
agreed.evidence: Lenz stated the rule in 1834. A magnet falls slowly in a copper pipe and quickly in a plastic pipe, and anyone can see it.

agreed.text: The best conductors, silver, copper, gold and aluminium, show the effect most. Plastic, wood and glass do not show it.
agreed.evidence: Swing a magnet over plates of different materials and count the swings. The better the conductor, the sooner the magnet stops.

agreed.text: Induction stoves heat pans with eddy currents and need a pan with a magnetic base.
agreed.evidence: Pans that hold a magnet firmly work on induction stoves. Pans that do not usually fail.

agreed.text: Stainless steel is a family of mixtures, and a magnet may stick to some kinds and not others, or to some places and not others.
agreed.evidence: Test a magnet on many tumblers, spoons and pans. The results differ, and engineers know the reasons.

challenging.claim: Aluminium is not affected by magnets at all.
challenging.for: A fridge magnet does not move or stick to aluminium foil, a can or a cooker.
challenging.against: A strong moving magnet makes an aluminium can roll, and a falling magnet slows down inside an aluminium tube. A very strong still magnet also attracts aluminium very faintly. 'Not attracted by a still magnet' is true. 'Not affected' is not.

challenging.claim: If a magnet does not stick to a metal, the metal has no iron in it.
challenging.for: Pure iron, and most steel, stick to a magnet.
challenging.against: Common stainless steel is mostly iron, yet a magnet hardly sticks to it, because nickel changes how the atoms are packed. A magnet that does not stick tells you little.

challenging.claim: A moving magnet attracts aluminium the way it attracts iron.
challenging.who: People who see a can roll after a magnet.
challenging.for: The can moves towards the magnet, as an iron nail would.
challenging.against: The push exists only while the magnet moves, and a held magnet does nothing. A can also stays behind a slow magnet. The force is a drag from eddy currents, not a pull on tiny magnets.

challenging.claim: A recycling centre sorts all its metal with magnets only.
challenging.who: Some people who have seen a scrapyard magnet.
challenging.for: Magnets lift steel out of a heap very well.
challenging.against: A magnet picks only the steel. The aluminium needs a separator that uses the moving-magnet effect. Then plastic, glass and paper need blowers, sieves, cameras or hands.

challenging.claim: A metal detector can find only magnetic metals.
challenging.for: Magnets find iron, and detectors are a bit like magnets.
challenging.against: A metal detector finds gold, silver, copper and aluminium too, because it senses the eddy currents they make, not an attraction.

challenging.claim: Hand sorting of waste is unskilled work that machines do better.
challenging.for: Machines sort quickly and need no break. Pickers face dirt and cuts.
challenging.against: Waste pickers recognise hundreds of materials by touch, sound and weight, and sort finer than many machines. In several Indian cities, picker cooperatives have been part of the city's waste system. Machines and pickers can work together.

challenging.claim: Every material is either magnetic or non-magnetic, with nothing in between.
challenging.for: It works for a fridge magnet and kitchen things.
challenging.against: Materials answer in three ways, and the answer can depend on temperature, shaping and whether the magnet moves. Many scientists see a scale, not two boxes.

big_questions.q: A still magnet ignores aluminium, and a moving magnet pushes it. Is aluminium magnetic or not?
big_questions.hint: Is a word like 'magnetic' about a material, or about a test?

big_questions.q: A still magnet does nothing to a metal such as aluminium. A moving magnet makes electricity in it. Can we say what a thing is without saying what is happening to it?
big_questions.hint: Think of yourself resting and yourself running. Which one is 'really' you?

big_questions.q: Iron stops being magnetic when it is red-hot, and aluminium reacts only when the magnet moves. What other labels at home are true only in some conditions?
big_questions.hint: Think of a hot day, a cold day, a loud room and a quiet room.

big_questions.q: In 1824, François Arago saw a compass needle turn above a spinning copper disc. Nobody could explain it for years. What should a scientist do with a result that nobody can explain?
big_questions.hint: Should they ignore it, hide it, or write it down?

big_questions.q: In some cities, waste pickers formed cooperatives so that they would be counted and paid fairly. Why do you think the people who sort our rubbish are often the last to be thanked?
big_questions.hint: Who sees the sorting, and who sees only the clean street?

big_questions.q: A magnet falls slowly through a copper pipe without touching it. What other things slow us down without touching us?
big_questions.hint: Think of the air, water, a crowd and a good mood.

big_questions.q: Everything responds a little to a magnet, even water. Is there anything in the world that responds to nothing at all?
big_questions.hint: What does 'responds' mean, and who decides how weak is too weak?

big_questions.q: An induction stove heats the pan, but not the glass or your hand. How can energy cross the air and warm only the pan?
big_questions.hint: What does the magnetic field carry? And what does the pan have that glass does not?

big_questions.q: A kabadiwala knows a metal by its ring when tapped, and a recycling centre knows it by a magnet and a camera. Who knows the metal better?
big_questions.hint: What can each way notice that the other cannot?

big_questions.q: You learn what a person is like partly by what they ignore and partly by how they respond when things move. Is that true of materials too?
big_questions.hint: Is a material's character the same whether it is still or moving?

story.title: The Cans That Jumped
story.note: A made-up story. Scrapyards in Madurai and elsewhere do sort steel, aluminium and plastic by hand, and eddy current separators that throw aluminium cans off a conveyor belt are real machines. Ilakkiya, her mother, the yard owner and the technician are made up.
text: At the edge of Madurai, behind a row of tea stalls, there was a scrap yard. It smelled of rust, rubber and old rain. Every morning, Ilakkiya's mother, Pappathi, sat on an upturned crate in front of a mountain of cans and bottles, with her sleeves rolled up. Her fingers were quick. Steel in this heap. Aluminium in that one. Plastic over there.

Ilakkiya was ten, and she loved the yard. After school she sat on the next crate and helped. She knew by touch which cans were light and which were heavy. She knew that the aluminium ones crumpled easily, and that the steel ones fought back.

The yard belonged to Mr Chinnasamy. He was proud of his new machine. It was an old crane with a big flat magnet on a chain, bought cheaply from a closing factory. When the crane swung over a heap of mixed rubbish, steel cans and nails jumped up and stuck to the magnet. The workers cheered every time.

But there was a problem. The magnet took only the steel. The aluminium cans, the plastic, the glass and the rubber all stayed behind in the same heap. And aluminium was the thing the buyers wanted most. A kilogram of aluminium cans paid three times as much as a kilogram of steel. Every day, Pappathi and the others picked the aluminium out by hand from the leftovers. It took hours.
'A magnet cannot take aluminium,' said Mr Chinnasamy, patting the crane. 'Everyone knows that. It is not magnetic. The magnet does not even see it.'

Ilakkiya had a strong silver magnet, as wide as a one-rupee coin, from a broken machine. She wore it on a string round her neck, as a toy. One afternoon, bored, she tied it to a longer thread and dangled it over a cola can, to see if anything would happen. Nothing did, of course. The magnet hung still.
She swung the thread. The magnet swung like a pendulum over the can, and then something odd happened. The can moved. Just a little. It rolled sideways, following the magnet.

She swung faster. The can rolled further. She tried a plastic bottle. It did not move at all. She tried a steel can, and the magnet snapped onto it with a click. She tried another aluminium can. It rolled, too.
She held the magnet still next to the can, holding her breath. Nothing happened. She swung it again. The can rolled.
'Amma, come and see,' she called. 'The aluminium cans move when the magnet moves.'
Pappathi came over, wiping her hands. She watched Ilakkiya swing the magnet three times. Her eyebrows went up. 'Show Mr Chinnasamy,' she said.
Mr Chinnasamy laughed. 'Child, aluminium is not magnetic. I have been in this business thirty years.' But Ilakkiya did not argue. She just held out the thread. 'Please, try it, sir. Just once.'

He took the thread. He swung it over a can, rather stiffly, because grown men do not like to be shown things by children. The can rolled. He swung it again. The can rolled again. He stopped swinging, and the can stopped. He started, and it moved.
'It is not stuck to the magnet,' said Ilakkiya. 'It only goes when the magnet goes. When the magnet stops, it stops. It is not being pulled like the steel. I think it is being dragged.'

The next week, a technician came to repair the crane. Her name was Hemalatha, and she wore a blue overall with her name sewn on it. Ilakkiya told her what she had seen. The technician did not laugh. She sat down on a crate and tried it herself. Then she was quiet for a long time.

'There is a machine for this,' she said at last. 'I have seen one in a big centre in Chennai. It has a drum full of magnets that spins very fast. The cans ride on a belt past the drum. The steel is already gone, so the drum ignores everything but the aluminium. The aluminium gets pushed forward, and jumps off the end of the belt into its own bin. The plastic just drops.'
'How does it know?' said Ilakkiya.

'It does not know,' said Hemalatha. 'It only moves the magnets very fast. A moving magnet makes little swirls of electricity inside any metal that carries electricity well. The swirls push back against the magnet. In plastic, there is nothing to swirl.' She smiled. 'You found it yourself, with a toy.'

It took two months and a lot of arguments, but the yard did build a small version. It was a cycle wheel with magnets stuck round its rim, spun by an old fan motor under the end of the belt. The first day it ran, the steel was already gone. The plastic bottles dropped straight down into a basket. And the aluminium cans leapt off the end of the belt one by one, like frogs, into the bin.

Pappathi stood watching with her arms folded and her sleeves still rolled up. Then she started to laugh. Mr Chinnasamy handed Ilakkiya the end of the thread. 'Your magnet,' he said. 'I think you should keep it.' And he asked her, quite seriously, whether she had any more ideas about the glass.
story.epiphany: A still magnet ignores aluminium, because aluminium has no lined-up tiny magnets. But a moving magnet makes swirling electric currents in aluminium, and these push against the magnet and drag the can along. That is why the cans rolled after the swinging magnet, and why a fast-spinning drum of magnets can throw aluminium cans off a belt while the plastic drops straight down.
ask: Why did the aluminium can not move when the magnet was held still, but did when the magnet swung?
Why did the plastic bottle never move, even when the magnet swung fast?
In the story, the steel cans were taken out first. Why was that needed before the spinning drum?
Ilakkiya noticed something that the owner, with thirty years of experience, did not expect. What helped her notice it?
Mr Chinnasamy did not want to try it at first. Why is it hard to test an idea that goes against what you are sure of?

experiments.title: Steel Detectives: where does a magnet stick on kitchen steel?
experiments.question: Does a magnet stick in the same way to all the steel in my kitchen? And does it stick in the same way to every part of one steel thing?
experiments.predict: Before you start, look at the steel things. For each spot, guess a score from 0 to 3 for how firmly the magnet will hold: 0 means not at all and 3 means firmly. Also guess which part of a tumbler will hold the magnet best: the rim, the wall or the base. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same magnet and press it for the same three seconds at every spot. We score each spot by how firmly the magnet holds, using the same 0 to 3 scale every time. Each spot is tested three times, because one try can be a fluke. Only the thing and the spot change, so any difference comes from the steel.

materials.item: a ceramic or bar magnet, or the strongest magnet you have
2 steel tumblers from different sets, and a steel katori
a steel spoon, and a steel plate or thali
a pan, kadai or pressure cooker with a flat base, steel if possible
the fridge door or an almirah door, and an aluminium vessel or foil, for the top and bottom of the scale
a pencil, a sheet of paper and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep the magnet away from phones, watches and bank cards. Keep magnets away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths. Hold vessels by the sides so nothing slips and drops on a foot.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then draw a tumbler and a spoon. Next to every spot you tested, write the middle score of its three tries. Colour the spots with a score of 2 or 3.

flow.do: Put the steel things on the table. Ask your child to guess a score from 0 to 3 for each spot, for how firmly the magnet will hold there. Ask which part of a tumbler will hold the magnet best. Write the guesses in the table.

ask.q: Which part of the tumbler do you think will hold the magnet best?
good: The base, because it is thickest.
All parts the same, because it is all steel.
The rim, because it is rolled.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Many children say all steel will stick the same. Write the guesses down to compare later.

flow.do: Set the scale. Press the magnet on the fridge door for three seconds, and try to pull it off with a light fingertip. Give it a 3. Do the same on the aluminium vessel, which is a 0. Say what a 1 and a 2 would feel like.

check.q: Why do we test the fridge door and the aluminium vessel before the steel things?
options: To set the top and bottom of our 0 to 3 scale
Because they are the biggest
To warm up the magnet
check.why: A score means something only if you know what the highest and lowest look like. The fridge door sets the 3 and the aluminium sets the 0. 'To warm up the magnet' is wrong. An engine needs warming up, but a magnet does not.

flow.parent: If your fridge door is stainless and the magnet does not stick, use an almirah or an iron gate for the 3.

flow.kid: Test the rim, the wall and the base. Three times each. Give each a score.

good: No, the rim holds differently from the wall.
Yes, it is the same steel everywhere.
The base is different from the wall.
