experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three things in a row, and draw an arrow for how far each rolled after a fast swish.

schedule.what: Tape a start line on a flat table. Test a still magnet on each thing. Swish slowly and fast five times each. Compare the three things. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you swish a strong magnet past an aluminium can, a plastic bottle and a steel tin. You find out which ones move, and when.

setup.art: A smooth table with a taped start line, a tape measure laid beside it and an aluminium can lying on its side.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a start line. Lay the can on its side on the line.

setup.art: A hand holding a magnet still 1 centimetre from the can, with nothing happening.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the magnet still next to the can for 10 seconds.

setup.art: A hand swishing the magnet quickly past the can, and the can rolling after it.
setup.caption: 3. Swish the magnet quickly past the can. Measure how far it rolls.

setup.art: A plastic bottle lying still and a steel tin leaping towards a still magnet.
setup.caption: 4. Try the plastic bottle and the steel tin in the same way.

setup.art: A bar chart of roll distances for the can, the bottle and the tin.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar for each thing, as long as its fast roll.

flow.do: Show your child the three things and the magnet. Ask what will happen to each thing when the magnet is held still, and when it is swished quickly past. Ask for a reason. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: Here is a strong magnet, an aluminium can, a plastic bottle and a steel tin. What will the magnet do to each when I hold it still? What about when I swish it quickly past? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You have a strong magnet and three things. What will happen to each thing if the magnet is still? What if it moves fast? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Do you think the aluminium can will move towards the magnet?
good: No, aluminium is not magnetic.
Yes, because it is a metal.
Only when the magnet moves.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Most children say the can will stay still, and some say it will move because it is metal. Write the guesses down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Can That Follows. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Wrap the magnet in thin cloth or tape. Tape a start line on the table and lay the can on its side on the line. Check the table is flat by seeing if the can stays still by itself.
flow.say: We need a flat, smooth table. Lay the can on its side. If it rolls by itself, move to a flatter place. A can that sits still means our test is fair.
flow.kid: Tape a start line. Lay the can on its side. Does it stay still by itself?
flow.parent: Keep the table away from steel legs, a steel sink or a gas cylinder, which can pull on a strong magnet. If the can drifts, put a thin cloth under it.
flow.context: In this step you tape a start line on a flat table and check the can stays still.

flow.do: Hold the magnet still 1 centimetre from the side of the can, for 10 seconds. Does the can move? Write yes or no. Do the same for the plastic bottle and the steel tin.
flow.say: Hold the magnet still, about a centimetre from the can. Wait ten seconds. Does it move? Now the bottle. Now the tin.
flow.kid: Hold the magnet still next to the can. Count to ten. Does it move?
flow.parent: The steel tin will roll towards the still magnet. The aluminium can and the plastic bottle should not move. Be ready to hold the magnet back so it does not snap onto the tin.
flow.context: In this step you hold the magnet still next to each thing and see which one moves.

flow.do: Lay the aluminium can on its start line. Swish the magnet slowly past it at about 1 centimetre away, five times. Measure the roll each time. Then swish it fast, five times. Take the middle roll for each speed.
flow.say: Now swish the magnet past the can, slowly, without touching. Measure how far the can rolls. Then swish it fast. Which speed makes the can roll further?
flow.kid: Swish the magnet past the can slowly. Measure the roll. Now swish fast. Measure again.

check.q: The aluminium can ignores a still magnet but rolls after a fast one. What is the best explanation?
options: The moving magnet makes swirls of electric current in the can, and these push against the magnet
The can has become a magnet like iron
The can is attracted by the air from the swish
check.why: A moving magnet makes eddy currents in a metal that carries electricity. These make their own magnetic field and drag the can along. Picking 'has become a magnet like iron' is wrong because a still magnet does nothing to the can. Picking 'the air' can be tested with a plastic bottle, which does not move.

flow.parent: A strong magnet swished at about 1 cm should make the can roll a few centimetres or more. A weak or slow magnet may only make the can wobble. If nothing moves, make the swish faster and the gap smaller, and write that down too.
flow.context: In this step you swish the magnet past the aluminium can slowly and fast, and measure the roll.

flow.do: Swish the magnet past the plastic bottle slowly and fast, five times each, and write the rolls. Then do the same for the steel tin, keeping the magnet from touching it.
flow.say: Now the plastic bottle, which is not a conductor. Does it move? And the steel tin. What is different about how it moves?
flow.kid: Swish the magnet past the plastic bottle. Does it move? Now the steel tin. What is different?

ask.q: How is the steel tin different from the aluminium can?
good: The tin moves towards a still magnet, and the can does not.
The tin sticks, and the can only follows when the magnet moves.
The tin is magnetic and the can is not.

flow.parent: The plastic bottle should not move at all. The steel tin is attracted even by a still magnet, so it rolls towards it whatever the speed. Keep the magnet from snapping onto the tin.
flow.context: In this step you test the plastic bottle and the steel tin, to compare them with the aluminium can.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then draw the three things in a row, with an arrow for how far each rolled after a fast swish.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a moving magnet pushes an aluminium can, though a still magnet does not. What I saw: the can rolled after a fast swish, the bottle did not, and the tin stuck to a still magnet. Why: a moving magnet makes swirling currents in the can, and the currents push back.
flow.context: In this last step you say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.title: The Pendulum That Stops: swing a magnet over four plates
experiments.question: A magnet swings on a thread over a wooden board, a plastic tray, an aluminium plate and a stainless steel plate. Over which will it stop soonest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, line up the four plates from the one you think will stop the magnet soonest to the one that will stop it last. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same magnet, the same thread and the same starting push each time. We keep the same small gap of about 2 millimetres between the magnet and the plate, by raising each plate on books. We count the swings until the magnet stops, three times for each plate. Only the plate changes, so any difference comes from the plate.

materials.item: a strong magnet, such as a neodymium disc or cube
40 centimetres of thread, and tape
a pencil, taped across the table edge to hold the thread
a wooden chopping board and a plastic tray, as flat as you can find
an aluminium plate or the thickest aluminium vessel you have, laid flat
a stainless steel plate or thali that a magnet does not stick to, and some books to raise the plates

experiments.safety: Strong magnets can chip or snap onto steel. Wrap the magnet in tape and do not let it hit the plates hard. Keep magnets away from children under five, phones and bank cards. If a magnet sticks to the steel plate, do not use that plate.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each plate, as tall as its middle number of swings.

schedule.what: Build the pendulum. Count swings with no plate, and over each of the four plates, three times each. Draw the bars. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you swing a magnet on a thread over four different plates. You count how many swings it takes to stop, and find out which plates slow it most.

setup.art: A pencil taped over a table edge, a thread hanging from it and a magnet taped to the end of the thread.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the magnet from the pencil on a 40 cm thread.

setup.art: A wooden board raised on books, with the magnet hanging 2 millimetres above it.
setup.caption: 2. Raise the board on books until the magnet just clears it.

setup.art: The magnet pulled 5 centimetres to one side, ready to be released over the board.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the magnet 5 cm to the side and let go. Count the swings.

setup.art: A bar chart with four bars for the wooden board, the plastic tray, the aluminium plate and the steel plate.
setup.caption: 4. Draw a bar for each plate.

flow.do: Show your child the plates and the magnet. Ask them to put the plates in order, from the one that will stop the magnet soonest to the one that will stop it last, and to give a reason. Write the order down.
flow.say: We will swing a magnet over four plates. Which plate do you think will stop it soonest? Which will stop it last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A magnet swings over four plates. Which stops it soonest? Which last? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that plate will stop the magnet soonest?
good: It is a metal.
It is the heaviest.
It is the roughest.

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Children often say the steel plate, because steel is the metal a magnet clings to. Write the order to compare later.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pendulum That Stops. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Tape the pencil across the table edge. Tie the thread to the pencil and tape the magnet to the other end, with a flat face pointing down. Raise the first plate on books until the magnet hangs about 2 millimetres above it.
flow.say: Hang the magnet from the pencil. Raise the plate on books until the magnet nearly touches it. We want the same small gap for every plate.
flow.kid: Hang the magnet on a thread. Raise the plate on books. The magnet should nearly touch it.
flow.parent: Keep the table away from steel. A gap of about 2 millimetres is the thickness of two coins stacked. Re-check the gap for each plate.
flow.context: In this step you build the pendulum and set the gap above the plate.

flow.do: First, swing the magnet with no plate under it. Pull it 5 cm to one side, let go, and count the swings until it stops or until you reach 30. Do it three times.
flow.say: First we need a number to compare with, called a baseline. Swing the magnet with no plate at all. How many swings does it make before it stops by itself?
flow.kid: Swing the magnet with no plate. Count the swings. Stop at 30.

check.q: Why do we swing the magnet with no plate first?
options: To see how long it swings when nothing is under it, so we can compare
To warm up the thread
To make the magnet stronger
check.why: A baseline shows how many swings the magnet makes by itself, because air and the thread also slow it. Without it, you could not tell how much of the slowing comes from the plate. 'To warm up the thread' is wrong. A sports player needs a warm-up, but a thread does not.

flow.context: In this step you swing the magnet with no plate, so that you have a count to compare with.

flow.do: Put the wooden board under the magnet. Pull the magnet 5 cm aside, let go and count the swings until it stops. Do it three times. Then do the same for the plastic tray, the aluminium plate and the steel plate. Write all the counts.
flow.say: Now the wooden board. Count the swings, three times. Then the plastic tray. Then the aluminium plate. Then the steel plate. Keep the gap the same.
flow.kid: Swing the magnet over each plate. Count the swings. Do it three times each.

ask.q: Which plate stopped the magnet soonest?
good: The aluminium plate.
The steel plate.
The plate that is a metal.

flow.parent: Expect the wooden board and plastic tray to give about the same count as no plate. The aluminium plate should stop the magnet in only a few swings. The stainless steel plate may give a smaller effect than aluminium. If a count is odd, repeat it and write both.
flow.context: In this step you swing the magnet over each plate and count the swings.

flow.do: Take the middle count for each plate. Draw one bar for each plate, as tall as its middle count.
flow.say: Take the middle of your three counts. Draw a bar for each plate. The shorter the bar, the sooner the plate stopped the magnet.
flow.kid: Find the middle count for each plate. Draw a bar for each. A short bar means a good stopper.
flow.context: In this step you turn your counts into a bar chart.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: metals that carry electricity well stop a swinging magnet. What I saw: the aluminium plate stopped it in a few swings, and the wood and plastic did not. Why: the moving magnet made swirling currents in the aluminium, and those pushed back.
flow.context: In this last step you say what you think, what you saw and why.

activities.title: Will It Work on an Induction Stove? Test with a magnet

materials.item: a magnet that is firm enough to hold on a fridge door
6 or more pans and vessels from the kitchen: a steel pan, an aluminium kadai, a cast iron tawa, a pressure cooker, a steel tumbler and a glass or clay dish
a sheet of paper with three boxes drawn on it: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick
a pencil

schedule.what: Guess which vessels would work on an induction stove. Press the magnet on the base of each. Sort the vessels into three boxes: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick.

activities.record: The sheet with three boxes: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick. The name of every vessel is written in one of the boxes, with a star next to the ones you guessed wrongly.
activities.context: In this short activity, you use a magnet to guess which of your vessels would work on an induction stove. You do not need an induction stove, and you do not use any heat.

setup.art: Six vessels in a row on a kitchen counter, with a magnet beside them and a sheet of paper with three boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Put the vessels in a row. Draw three boxes on a sheet.

setup.art: A hand pressing a magnet on the flat base of a pan turned upside down.
setup.caption: 2. Turn each vessel over. Press the magnet on its base.

setup.art: Vessels placed into three boxes according to how firmly the magnet held.
setup.caption: 3. Put each vessel in a box: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, or does not stick.

flow.do: Put the vessels on the counter. Ask your child to guess which ones would heat on an induction stove, and why. Write the guesses on the sheet.
flow.say: An induction stove heats a pan using magnets and electricity, with no flame. Which of these vessels do you think would work on it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which vessels would heat on an induction stove? Guess. Why?

ask.q: Which vessel do you think will work best on an induction stove?
good: The steel pan, because it is steel.
The aluminium kadai, because it is a metal.
The cast iron tawa, because it is iron.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Do not use the stove for this activity. A magnet gives a rough guide only, and the maker's instructions are the final word.
flow.context: This is the first step of Will It Work on an Induction Stove? You guess before you test.

flow.do: Turn each vessel over. Press the magnet on the flat part of its base for three seconds. Try a light pull. Write whether it sticks firmly, weakly or not at all.
flow.say: Turn each vessel over. Press the magnet on the flat base for three seconds. Does it hold firmly? Or only a little? Or not at all?
flow.kid: Turn the vessel over. Press the magnet on the base. Does it stick?

check.q: A magnet sticks firmly to the base of a pan. What does this say about using it on an induction stove?
options: The pan will probably heat well, because its base is magnetic steel
The pan will not work
The pan will melt
check.why: An induction stove heats a pan with a magnetic base well. A pan that holds a magnet firmly usually works. Picking 'melt' mixes up the stove with a flame, and there is no flame.

flow.context: In this step you press the magnet on the base of each vessel.

flow.do: Sort the vessels into the three boxes: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick. Mark a star next to every vessel that did not match your guess.
flow.say: Which vessels went into each box? Were any of your guesses wrong? Which one surprised you?
flow.kid: Sort the vessels into three boxes. Which one surprised you?

good: The steel tumbler, because it did not stick.
The aluminium kadai, because it did not stick.
The pressure cooker, because the base was different from the sides.

flow.parent: Aluminium and copper should not stick. A cast iron tawa should hold firmly. Stainless steel varies. Pans made for induction cooking usually hold a magnet firmly on the base. A vessel might stick on the sides and not on the base, or the other way round.
flow.context: In this step you sort the vessels into three boxes: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick.

flow.do: Ask your child to say one sentence about what the magnet can and cannot tell you about a vessel.
flow.say: A magnet test is a quick guide. What can it tell us about a pan? And what can it not tell us?
flow.kid: What can the magnet tell you about a pan? What can it not tell you?
flow.think: A magnet that sticks says the base is magnetic steel. A magnet that does not stick does not say what the vessel is made of. Why not?
flow.context: In this last step you think about what the magnet test can and cannot tell you.

activities.title: Ask a Kabadiwala or Waste Picker: how do you tell metals apart?

materials.item: a grown-up to go with your child
a notebook and a pencil, with five questions written in it
a magnet in a plastic bag
a small bag of four test things: a steel spoon, an aluminium foil ball, a brass key and a copper wire
soap and water, for washing hands afterwards

schedule.what: Write five questions. Visit a kabadiwala, a scrap dealer or a waste picker with a grown-up. Listen. Write down how they tell metals apart. Compare with what you know.

activities.record: The notebook with the five questions and the answers, and one drawing of a way of telling metals apart that you did not know before.
activities.context: In this activity, you ask someone who sorts metal for a living how they tell iron, aluminium, brass and copper apart. You compare their ways with the magnet tests in this unit.

setup.art: A child with a notebook asking questions to a scrap dealer at a shop with heaps of metal.
setup.caption: 1. Ask your five questions politely. Listen to the answers.

setup.art: A scrap dealer tapping a brass vessel and listening to the ring while a child watches.
setup.caption: 2. Watch how they tell metals apart: by sound, weight, colour or a magnet.

setup.art: A page in a notebook with drawings of a magnet, a tapping hand and a hand weighing a piece of metal.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the ways of telling metals apart that you learned.

flow.do: Ask your child to write five questions for a metal sorter. Help with ideas, such as these. How do you tell iron from aluminium? How do you tell brass from copper? Which metal is worth most? What do you do with a magnet?
flow.say: People who sort metal every day know many things we do not. What would you like to ask them? Write five questions.
flow.kid: Write five questions for a metal sorter. How do they tell metals apart?

ask.q: What do you think a sorter does to tell iron from aluminium?
good: Uses a magnet.
Lifts the piece, because aluminium is lighter.
Taps it and listens.

flow.parent: Choose a kabadiwala, scrap dealer or waste picker your family already knows or can reach safely, and go with your child. Ask permission before you ask questions or take notes. Do not take photographs without asking.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask a Kabadiwala or Waste Picker. You write your questions.

flow.do: Visit the sorter with your child. Be polite and listen. Ask the five questions, and write down the answers. If they agree, ask them to sort your four test things and say how they know.
flow.say: Thank you for talking to us. We are learning about metals and magnets. How do you tell different metals apart? Could you show us with these four things?
flow.kid: Ask your questions politely. Listen carefully. Write the answers.
flow.parent: Stay by your child. Do not touch sharp or dirty scrap. Treat the person as an expert, because they are. Offer a small thanks, such as chai or a few rupees for their time, if appropriate. If they say no, that is fine.
flow.context: In this step you visit a metal sorter and ask your questions.

flow.do: At home, wash hands. Compare what the sorter said with what this unit says. Which of their ways use a magnet? Which use sound, weight or colour? Which ways did they know that we did not?
flow.say: What did they say that you did not know? Which of their ways match what we learned about magnets? Which are completely different?
flow.kid: What did the sorter tell you? Which ways use a magnet? Which do not?

check.q: A sorter says, 'I tap it. Brass rings long and warm, and steel rings short and dull.' Is this a good way to tell them apart?
options: Yes, because different metals ring differently, and a trained ear can hear it
No, because only magnets can tell metals apart
No, because sound has nothing to do with metal
check.why: Different metals and shapes ring differently when tapped. People who handle metal every day learn to hear the difference. A magnet is one way, and sound is another. 'Only magnets' comes from the mistaken idea that a magnet is the only test.

flow.context: In this step you compare the sorter's ways with the magnet tests in this unit.

flow.do: Draw one way of telling metals apart that you did not know before. Write one sentence under it.
flow.say: Draw the new way you learned. Write one sentence about it.
flow.kid: Draw a new way you learned. Write one sentence.
flow.think: A sorter and a recycling centre both sort metal. What can the sorter do that the machine cannot?
flow.context: In this last step you draw the new way you learned.

activities.title: Three Columns: sort the world by how it answers a magnet

materials.item: 20 small cards, cut from paper, for the things below
a big sheet of paper with three columns drawn on it
a pencil and a ruler
scissors, used by a grown-up for the cards

schedule.what: Write 20 cards. Guess the column for each. Check with the key. Talk about the surprises.

activities.record: The big sheet with three columns and all 20 cards laid out, and a ring around the cards you got wrong.
activities.context: In this activity, you sort twenty things into three columns by what a very strong magnet would do to them: attract them strongly, attract them very weakly, or push them away very weakly.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with three columns marked strong pull, tiny pull and tiny push.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three columns on a big sheet.

setup.art: Twenty small cards with names of materials written on them, in a heap.
setup.caption: 2. Write the name of a thing on each card.

setup.art: Cards laid out in the three columns with some rings drawn around those that moved.
setup.caption: 3. Put each card in a column. Check with the key.

flow.do: Write twenty things on cards. Use iron, nickel, cobalt, a steel nail, aluminium, magnesium, platinum, the oxygen in the air and titanium. Add copper, gold, silver, water, wood, glass, a diamond, lead, zinc, bismuth and your own hand.
flow.say: A very strong magnet pulls a few of these a lot. It pulls some a tiny bit, and pushes the rest a tiny bit. Write each name on a card. Then guess which column each belongs in.
flow.kid: Write the twenty names on cards. Guess where each one goes.
flow.parent: Bismuth is a brittle silvery metal, and the strongest of the pushed-away materials. The oxygen in the air is pulled a tiny bit. The key that you read out later gives the column for everything else in the list.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Columns. You write the cards.

flow.do: Lay the cards in the three columns by guessing. Say a reason out loud for each guess.
flow.say: Put each card where you think it belongs. Say your reason. Do not worry about being wrong. We will check in a minute.
flow.kid: Put each card in a column. Say why.

ask.q: Which things do you think are pulled strongly by a magnet?
good: Iron and steel.
Nickel and cobalt.
All the metals.

flow.context: In this step you guess the column for each card.

flow.do: Read out the key. Strong pull: iron, nickel, cobalt, a steel nail. Tiny pull: aluminium, magnesium, platinum, titanium and the oxygen in the air. Tiny push: copper, gold, silver, water, wood, glass, a diamond, lead, zinc, bismuth and your own hand. Move the cards that were wrong.
flow.say: Here is what scientists have measured. Move any card that is in the wrong column. How many of your guesses were right?
flow.kid: Move any card that is wrong. How many were right?

check.q: Which column holds most of the things in your kitchen, including your own hand?
options: Very weakly pushed away
Strongly pulled
Very weakly pulled
check.why: Most materials, including water, wood, copper and your own body, are pushed away extremely weakly by a magnet. 'Strongly pulled' comes from the mistaken idea that all metals are magnetic.

flow.context: In this step you check your guesses against the key and move the cards.

flow.do: Ask your child which cards surprised them most, and why. Then ask whether there is a card in the 'tiny push' column that is also a metal. Count how many of the metals are in each column.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? How many metals are in the tiny push column? Can a metal be pushed away by a magnet?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you most? Are there metals in the tiny push column?
flow.think: A fridge magnet cannot show the tiny pulls and pushes. A huge magnet can. Are the tiny pulls and pushes there even when nobody measures them?
flow.context: In this last step you talk about which cards surprised you.

activities.title: Plan a Sorting Line on Paper

materials.item: a big sheet of paper and a pencil
8 small cards for the heap: a steel can, an aluminium can, a plastic bottle, a glass jar, a brass key, a sheet of paper, a rubber slipper and a copper wire
4 cards for the machines: Magnet, Spinning Magnet Drum, Air Blower and Hands
a ruler and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw a conveyor belt. Decide the order of the four machines. Run the eight waste cards through your line. Explain your design.

activities.record: The drawing of your sorting line, with the four machines in order, and a list of what ended up in each bin.
activities.context: In this activity, you plan the order of the machines in a recycling centre on paper. You use what a magnet and a spinning magnet drum do to sort a heap of mixed waste.

setup.art: A long drawn conveyor belt on a big sheet with a heap of mixed waste at the start.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a conveyor belt with a heap at the start.

setup.art: Four machine cards placed along the belt in a chosen order.
setup.caption: 2. Place the four machine cards along the belt.

setup.art: Eight waste cards moved along the belt and into bins at the end.
setup.caption: 3. Run each card through the line. Which bin does it end up in?

flow.do: Lay out the eight waste cards and the four machine cards. Explain what each machine does. The Magnet lifts steel. The Spinning Magnet Drum throws aluminium, brass and copper off the belt. The Air Blower lifts light paper and film. Hands pick everything else.
flow.say: A recycling centre has four stations. The Magnet lifts steel. The Spinning Drum throws off aluminium, brass and copper. The Blower lifts light paper. Hands pick the rest. In what order would you put them?
flow.kid: There are four machines. Which should come first? Which should come last? Guess.

ask.q: Which machine do you think should come first?
good: The magnet, to take out steel.
The blower, to take out paper.
The hands, to take out big things.

flow.parent: In a real centre, the steel is taken out first, so it does not stick to the spinning drum. Let your child guess before you tell them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plan a Sorting Line. You learn what each machine does.

flow.do: Draw the belt on the big sheet. Place the four machine cards along it in the order your child chooses. Ask them to explain why each machine is where it is.
flow.say: Put the machines along the belt. Explain why each one goes where it does. What goes wrong if two are swapped?
flow.kid: Put the four machines along the belt. Say why each goes where it does.

check.q: Why does a real centre take the steel out before the spinning magnet drum?
options: Steel would stick to the drum, since a still magnet attracts it
Steel is too heavy to travel on the belt
Steel makes the drum rust
check.why: A magnet drum would grab steel cans and hold them. The steel must be taken out first. Picking 'too heavy' mixes up weight with magnetism.

flow.context: In this step you place the four machines along the belt and explain your order.

flow.do: Run each of the eight waste cards through your line, one at a time. Say which machine takes it out, and put it in a bin at the end. Mark any card that goes wrong.
flow.say: Take the steel can first. Which machine takes it out? Then the aluminium can. Then the plastic bottle. Go card by card.
flow.kid: Run each card along the belt. Which machine takes it out?
flow.parent: Expected: the steel can is lifted by the Magnet. The aluminium can, the brass key and the copper wire are thrown by the Drum. The paper goes with the Blower. The plastic bottle, the glass jar and the rubber slipper are picked by Hands, or fall off the end.
flow.context: In this step you run each waste card through your line.

flow.do: Talk about the people who work in a centre like this. Ask: where in the line does a person do something that a machine cannot?
flow.say: A machine cannot tell a glass jar from a clear plastic jar. Who does? What would happen to this line without them?
flow.kid: Which jobs on the line need a person? Why?
flow.think: In India, waste pickers often do the sorting by hand. Where on this line would their skill help most?
flow.context: In this last step you think about the people who work in sorting.

activities.title: Does Rust Stick? An old nail and its flakes

materials.item: an old rusty nail, bolt or iron tool, and a new clean nail
a magnet wrapped in a thin plastic bag
a sheet of white paper and a spoon
soap and water, for washing hands afterwards

schedule.what: Guess whether rust sticks. Test the rusty nail and its flakes with a wrapped magnet. Explain what you found.

activities.record: A short table: new nail, rusty nail, rust flakes, and whether each stuck to the magnet. A drawing of the rusty nail cut in half.
activities.context: In this activity, you test a rusty nail and the brown flakes that fall off it with a magnet, to find out what a magnet can see in rust.

setup.art: A clean new nail and a rusty old nail side by side on white paper.
setup.caption: 1. Put a new nail and a rusty nail on the paper.

setup.art: A magnet in a plastic bag touching the rusty nail, which clings to it.
setup.caption: 2. Test each nail with the wrapped magnet.

setup.art: A grown-up scraping brown flakes from a nail onto a sheet of white paper with a spoon.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up scrapes some rust flakes onto the paper. Test them.

flow.do: Show your child the two nails. Ask them to guess if each will stick to the magnet, and whether the rust flakes will stick too. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Rust is what iron turns into when it stays wet. Will a magnet stick to a rusty nail? And to the flakes of rust? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the magnet stick to the rusty nail? And to the rust flakes? Why?

ask.q: Do you think rust is still magnetic?
good: Yes, because it is still iron.
No, because it has changed into something else.
Only partly.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Rusty nails can cut skin. A grown-up handles them and scrapes the flakes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Does Rust Stick? You guess before you test.

flow.do: Touch the wrapped magnet to the new nail and then to the rusty nail. Lift each one. Write whether it sticks.
flow.say: Touch the magnet to the clean nail. Now to the rusty one. Which sticks? Do they both stick?
flow.kid: Touch the magnet to each nail. Does it stick? Write it down.
flow.parent: Both nails should stick, because the core of each is still iron. If the rusty nail is very eaten away, it may be weaker.
flow.context: In this step you test the clean nail and the rusty nail.

flow.do: A grown-up scrapes a spoonful of brown flakes from the rusty nail onto white paper. Hold the wrapped magnet just above the flakes, then touch it to them. Do any flakes jump or stick? Then pull the magnet out of its bag over the paper, so that whatever stuck drops off.
flow.say: These flakes are the rust itself. Hold the magnet just above them. Do they jump? Touch it to them. How many stick?
flow.kid: Hold the magnet above the flakes. Do any jump up?

check.q: The rusty nail sticks to a magnet, but most of the rust flakes do not. What is the best reason?
options: Under the rust there is still iron, but the rust itself is only weakly magnetic
The flakes are too light for a magnet to feel
A magnet works only on whole objects, not on powder
check.why: Rust is iron joined with oxygen and water. Most forms are only weakly magnetic. The nail still has an iron core that the magnet feels. Picking 'too light' is tempting, but a magnet can pick up fine black sand.

flow.parent: Many rust flakes stick faintly or not at all, though some dark ones may. Write what you see. Wash hands after handling rust.
flow.context: In this step you test the rust flakes with the wrapped magnet.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the rusty nail cut in half, with the iron core and the rust coat. Ask one sentence about what a magnet can and cannot tell about rust.
flow.say: Draw the nail cut in half. Show the iron in the middle and the rust outside. What does the magnet feel?
flow.kid: Draw the nail cut in half. Where is the iron? Where is the rust?
flow.think: A magnet finds iron that is still iron. Can it find iron that has turned to rust?
flow.context: In this last step you draw the inside of a rusty nail and think about what the magnet feels.

projects.title: Our Kitchen's Metal Map: a poster of what sticks

materials.item: a magnet that holds firmly on a fridge door
a notebook and a pencil, for the table of at least 20 kitchen things
a big sheet of paper and markers
a few small sticky notes or pieces of tape
a grown-up who agrees which things may be tested

projects.safety: Test only things a grown-up agrees to. Do not test knives or anything sharp. Keep magnets away from phones, watches and bank cards.

schedule.what: Make a table of at least 20 kitchen things. Test each with the magnet and write the result.
Draw the poster with three zones. Stick it on the fridge. Teach the family one new thing from it.

projects.record: The table of 20 kitchen things and their results, and the poster.
projects.context: In this project, you test twenty things in your kitchen with a magnet and make a poster of what sticks, so that the whole family can use it. It brings together what this unit says about steel, aluminium and brass.

setup.art: A table with twenty rows of kitchen things and columns for guess and result.
setup.caption: 1. Make a table of 20 kitchen things.

setup.art: A child pressing a magnet on a pan, a tumbler and a spoon in turn.
setup.caption: 2. Test each thing and write the result.

setup.art: A big poster on the fridge with three coloured zones and drawings of kitchen things in each.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a poster with three zones and stick it on the fridge.

flow.do: Help your child make a table of at least 20 kitchen things. Include a pressure cooker, tawa, kadai, spoon, tumbler and katori. Add a plate, a steel lid, aluminium foil, a brass lamp, a copper pot and a glass jar. Ask for a guess for each.
flow.say: We will make a map of our kitchen. First list twenty things. Then guess which will stick to the magnet and which will not. Write your guess for each.
flow.kid: Make a list of 20 kitchen things. Guess which will stick. Write the guesses.

ask.q: Which kitchen things do you think will not stick?
good: Things made of aluminium.
Things made of wood or plastic.
Some steel things.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Children usually expect all metal to stick. Write the guesses in pencil.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Metal Map. You make a list and guess.

flow.do: Test each thing with the magnet. Press it for three seconds on a flat part and give a score. Give 3 for firm, 2 for holds but easily pulled off, 1 for a tiny tug, and 0 for nothing. Write the result next to the guess.
flow.say: Test each thing. Press the magnet for three seconds. Give it a score from 0 to 3. Write it next to your guess.
flow.kid: Test each thing with the magnet. Score it from 0 to 3. Write the score.

check.q: A steel bowl scores 0, and an aluminium pot scores 0. Does that mean they are made of the same material?
options: No, a score of 0 only says they are not strongly attracted. Many materials score 0
Yes, both are metal
Yes, both are shiny
check.why: A 0 says only that a still magnet does not hold on. Stainless steel, aluminium, copper, brass, plastic, glass and wood can all score 0. The magnet cannot tell them apart.

flow.context: In this step you test every thing in your list and write the scores.

flow.do: On day 1, look at the finished table. Count how many things scored 3, 2 or 1, and how many scored 0. How many guesses were right? Pick the three things that surprised you most.
flow.say: Count how many scored 3, how many 2, how many 1, and how many 0. Which guesses were wrong? Which three things surprised you?
flow.kid: Count the scores. How many things stick firmly? How many do not stick?
flow.wait: Come back tomorrow to make the poster.
flow.context: In this step you count the results and find the surprises.

flow.do: On day 2, draw the poster on the big sheet with three zones: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick. Draw or write each thing in its zone. Add a note: an induction stove needs a pan that holds a magnet firmly on its base.
flow.say: Draw the map of our kitchen. Make three zones. Put each thing in its zone. Add a note for the induction stove.
flow.kid: Draw a poster with three zones. Put each kitchen thing in its zone.
flow.parent: Make the poster large, with clear drawings, so it is useful to the whole family. Add a line saying that a magnet test cannot tell which metal a thing is made of.
flow.context: On day 2, you draw the poster with the three zones.

flow.do: Stick the poster on the fridge. Ask your child to teach one new thing from the poster to another family member.
flow.say: Show the poster to someone at home. Teach them one thing they did not know. What will you tell them?
flow.kid: Show your poster. Teach someone one new thing.
flow.think: Who in your family would find this poster most useful, and why?
flow.context: In this last step you stick up the poster and teach someone.

challenges.title: Six Mystery Pieces: name them with the fewest tests
challenges.problem: A helper gives you six mystery pieces of metal, numbered 1 to 6. You may use three kinds of test: a magnet, colour, and the sound when you tap or drop the piece. Draw a flowchart with the fewest questions that names every piece, then check it.
constraints: Use only these tests: the magnet, colour and sound. No scratching and no heating.
Each test is a yes or no question, for example 'Does the magnet stick?'
Your flowchart must reach a name for every one of the six pieces.
No piece may take more than three questions.
materials: six metal pieces chosen by a helper: for example an iron nail, a steel spoon, an aluminium foil piece, a copper wire, a brass key and a stainless steel katori
a hard floor or tile, to drop the pieces on
a big sheet of paper and a pencil for the flowchart
a helper to check the answers
general: Ask about the magnet first, to split the pieces into two groups.
Ask about colour next, to split each group again.
Use the sound test to tell apart two pieces that look and feel alike.
creative: Put the question that splits the pieces most evenly first, so that fewer questions are needed.
Add a fourth kind of test if you can, such as how heavy the piece feels, and see if it removes a question.
Draw a second flowchart with a different order of questions, and see which one is shorter.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your flowchart. Test it on all six pieces. Count the questions each piece needed. Can you find a shorter flowchart? Which question was most useful?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about using tests wisely. You find the fewest questions that name six mystery metals.

setup.art: Six numbered metal pieces in a row on a table beside a magnet.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the six pieces. Guess what each may be.

setup.art: A flowchart on paper with boxes that say Does the magnet stick? and lines for yes and no.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a flowchart of yes or no questions.

setup.art: A hand tapping a piece on a tile floor and an ear turned towards it.
setup.caption: 3. Test the pieces and name them.

flow.do: A helper chooses the six pieces and numbers them in secret. Look at them with your child. Ask them to guess what each piece is made of, and which test would help most.
flow.say: Here are six mystery pieces. Which test would split them into two groups most evenly? Think before you begin.
flow.kid: Six mystery pieces. Which test splits them best? Guess.

ask.q: What is the best first question to ask about the pieces?
good: Does the magnet stick?
What colour is it?
Does it ring when I tap it?

flow.context: This is the first step of Six Mystery Pieces. You look and plan.

flow.do: Test all six pieces with the magnet, then by colour, then by sound. Write the results in a table, one row for each piece.
flow.say: Test each piece three ways. Write the results in a table. Then look at the table and see which test splits the pieces most evenly.
flow.kid: Test each piece with the magnet, by colour and by sound. Write the results in a table.

check.q: Colour splits six pieces into 3 and 3. The magnet test splits them into 2 and 4. Which is usually the better first question for a short flowchart?
options: The magnet test, because it always gives the shortest chart
Colour, because 3 and 3 is the more even split
It makes no difference which is first
check.why: A test that splits the pieces more evenly tends to give a shorter flowchart. But a short chart also depends on the later questions, so try both orders and count the questions.

flow.context: In this step you test all six pieces three ways.

flow.do: Draw a flowchart. Start with the question you chose. Draw a box for each question and arrows for yes and no. Make sure every piece reaches a name in three questions or fewer.
flow.say: Draw your flowchart. Start with the question you think is best. Each piece must end at a name in three questions or fewer.
flow.kid: Draw a flowchart of yes or no questions. Every piece must end at a name.
flow.parent: Check each branch. If two pieces share a path, the flowchart needs another question. Let your child find the problem before you say.
flow.context: In this step you draw the flowchart.

flow.do: Run each piece through your flowchart. Ask the helper to say whether each name is right. Count how many questions each piece took, and the total.
flow.say: Run each piece through your chart. The helper tells you if you are right. How many questions did you need in all?
flow.kid: Run each piece through your chart. Were you right? How many questions did you need?
flow.think: A magnet is very good at saying yes to iron. It is bad at telling brass from copper. Which test is best for that job?
flow.context: In this last step you check your flowchart against the answers.

challenges.title: The Pocket Induction Tester: a card that checks a pan in ten seconds
challenges.problem: A shopkeeper wants to help customers check whether a pan will work on an induction stove, without a stove in the shop. Design a pocket tester from a card, a magnet and a string, with instructions that anyone can follow in ten seconds.
constraints: The tester must use only a magnet and things on a card, with no electricity.
A person must be able to use it after reading no more than five short lines.
It must give one of three answers: works, may work or will not work.
Test it on at least 8 vessels.
materials: a flat magnet that holds firmly on a fridge door
a stiff card or piece of cardboard
8 or more pans and vessels from your kitchen or neighbours
general: Tape the magnet to a card and write 'Press this on the base of the pan.'
Give three answers on the card: holds firmly, holds weakly and does not hold.
Add a picture of a pan with a magnet pressed to its base.
creative: Add a string with a small weight to the card. The user tilts the pan so that an edge of its base lifts off the table, and presses the magnet on the base. If the magnet holds, the pan works.
Draw colours on the card: green for holds firmly, yellow for weak and red for none.
Add a warning that the maker's label is the final word, since a magnet only tells you about the base.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your tester. Make it and test it on 8 vessels. Ask someone to use it without your help. Could they follow the instructions? Change the card and test again.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about using a simple tool for a real job. You make a magnet-based tester that anyone can use.

setup.art: A card with a magnet taped to it, a string and short instructions written below.
setup.caption: 1. Make the card, with the magnet taped on and short instructions.

setup.art: A hand pressing the card's magnet on the base of a pan, with the card showing three answers.
setup.caption: 2. Press the magnet on the base of a pan and read the answer.

setup.art: A table with 8 vessels and ticks and crosses written beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Test the tester on 8 vessels and write the results.

flow.do: Read the problem. Ask your child to sketch a tester and to say what the three answers should mean.
flow.say: A shopkeeper wants a ten-second tester for pans. What should it look like? What should the three answers say? Draw an idea first.
flow.kid: Draw a pocket tester for pans. What are the three answers?

ask.q: What will the tester tell the customer when the magnet holds firmly on the base?
good: The pan will probably work.
The base is magnetic steel.
Buy it for the induction stove.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Pocket Induction Tester. You plan.

flow.do: Build the tester. Tape the magnet on the card, and write the five lines of instructions. Test it on 8 vessels and write down what it says for each.
flow.say: Build your tester. Write the instructions. Test it on eight vessels. What does it say for each one?
flow.kid: Build the card. Test it on 8 vessels. Write what it says.

check.q: A pan's sides hold a magnet well, but its base does not. Would the pan work on an induction stove?
options: Probably not, because the base touches the stove and must be magnetic
Yes, because the sides are magnetic
Yes, because the whole pan is steel
check.why: The stove heats the part of the pan that sits on it, which is the base. If the base is not magnetic steel, the pan will heat badly. So the tester must be pressed on the base.

flow.context: In this step you build the tester and try it on 8 vessels.

flow.do: Ask someone else to use the card without your help. Watch where they get stuck. Change the lines on the card to fix it. Test again with the same person.
flow.say: Give the card to someone, and say nothing. Watch what they do. Where did they get stuck? Change the lines.
flow.kid: Give the card to someone. Watch. Fix any line that confused them.
flow.parent: Resist helping. A good tester works without the maker beside it.
flow.context: In this step you test your card on someone else and improve it.

flow.do: Write one line saying what the tester cannot tell. For example, a magnet cannot tell if the pan is the right size, and the maker's label is the final word.
flow.say: What can your tester not tell the customer? Write it on the card.
flow.kid: What can the tester not tell? Write it on the card.
flow.think: A good tool says what it cannot do, as well as what it can. Why does that make it more useful?
flow.context: In this last step you add a line about what the tester cannot tell.

worksheets.title: How Materials Answer a Magnet, Class 4 (core)

items.p: A fridge magnet is held still against an aluminium can. What happens?
opts: Nothing, because a still magnet does not attract aluminium
items.why: Aluminium is not a magnetic material, so a still magnet does not hold it. Picking 'sticks firmly' is the idea that all metals stick.

items.p: A strong magnet is swished quickly past an aluminium can that lies on its side. What is most likely to happen?
opts: The can rolls after the magnet
Nothing, because aluminium is not magnetic
The can jumps onto the magnet and sticks
The can is pushed away from the magnet
items.why: A moving magnet makes swirling electric currents in the can. These make a magnetic field that drags the can along. A still magnet does nothing, but a moving one does.

items.p: A swirl of electric current that a moving magnet makes inside a piece of metal is called an ____ current.
items.why: An eddy is a small whirl, like the one you see in a river behind a rock.

items.p: A plastic bottle rolls after a fast-moving magnet just as an aluminium can does.
items.why: False. Plastic does not carry electricity, so no swirls of current form in it. A fast-moving magnet does not move a plastic bottle.

items.p: Which of these carries electricity best, and so drags a moving magnet most?
items.why: Copper is one of the best conductors of electricity, so strong swirls form in it. Wood, glass and rubber do not carry electricity.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Ferromagnetic
strongly attracted by a still magnet
Paramagnetic
attracted extremely weakly by a very strong magnet
Diamagnetic
pushed away extremely weakly by a very strong magnet
Eddy current
a swirl of electricity made in metal by a moving magnet
Conductor
a material that lets electricity pass easily
items.why: These five words are the vocabulary of the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each.

items.p: Sort each thing by what a magnet does to it: a still magnet attracts it strongly, a fast-moving magnet is dragged by it, or neither.
items.why: Iron and steel are attracted even by a still magnet. Copper and aluminium carry electricity well and drag a moving magnet. Wood and plastic do neither.

items.p: A recycling centre must take steel cans out of a heap before it uses a spinning magnet drum to throw aluminium off the belt. Why?
opts: Steel would stick to the drum, since a still magnet attracts it
items.why: A drum of magnets would grab the steel and hold it. So a magnet takes out the steel first.

items.p: A pan works well on an induction stove when a magnet sticks ____ to its base.
items.why: A base of magnetic steel heats well in the changing magnetic field of the stove.

items.p: Three of these are pulled by a still magnet. Which one is not?
items.why: Iron, nickel and cobalt are the three common magnetic metals. Aluminium is not attracted by a still magnet.

items.p: A friend says that a steel tumbler must be non-magnetic because a magnet did not stick to its wall. Explain what might still be true.
items.a: A stainless steel tumbler might be made of a kind of stainless steel that a magnet does not stick to, though it still has iron in it. The magnet may stick a little at the bent rim or base.
items.why: A strong answer says that stainless steel is a family and that bending can change the magnetism.

items.p: If a magnet does not stick to a metal, the metal has no iron in it.
items.why: False. Common stainless steel is mostly iron, but its mixture means a magnet hardly sticks.

items.p: A metal detector beeps over a buried brass key. Brass is not attracted by a still magnet. How can the detector find it?
opts: It senses the eddy currents the changing magnetic field makes in the key
It senses the key's tiny magnets
items.why: The detector makes a changing magnetic field. This field makes eddy currents in any metal that carries electricity, and the detector senses them.

items.p: Explain in your own words why a magnet falls slowly in a thick copper pipe but quickly in a plastic pipe.
items.a: As the magnet falls, it makes swirling electric currents in the copper. These make a magnetic field that pushes up against the falling magnet and slows it. Plastic does not carry electricity, so nothing pushes up.
items.why: A strong answer says that swirls form in the copper only and that they push against the movement.

items.p: Draw a flat aluminium plate with a magnet moving above it. Draw curved arrows in the plate to show the swirls of current, and an arrow to show which way the magnet moves.
items.a: A flat plate with a magnet above it and an arrow for its motion. Inside the plate, curved loops of arrows swirl under the magnet.
items.why: The swirls form in the plate under the moving magnet. Without movement, there are no swirls.
items.art: A blank flat plate drawn in side view.

items.p: A magnet swings over a wooden board, a plastic tray and an aluminium plate. Over which does it stop in the fewest swings?
items.why: Swirls of current form only in the aluminium, and they push against the swinging magnet. Wood and plastic do nothing.

items.p: A thin sheet of aluminium foil and a thick aluminium plate are both under a swinging magnet. Which stops it sooner, and why?
opts: The thick plate, because more metal gives the swirls more room
The foil, because it is lighter
Neither, because aluminium is not magnetic
items.why: A thick plate has more room for eddy currents to flow, so the push is stronger. 'Not magnetic' only applies to a still magnet.

items.p: Cuts are made in a copper plate so that the swirls cannot loop round. What happens to the drag on a moving magnet?
items.why: The swirls need unbroken paths to flow round. Slits stop them, so the push on the magnet falls.

items.p: Put the steps of the chain of events in order, from the moving magnet to the dragged can.
items: The magnet moves past the can
Electric currents swirl inside the can
The swirls make a magnetic field in the can
The can's field drags the can after the magnet
a: The magnet moves past the can
Electric currents swirl inside the can
The swirls make a magnetic field in the can
The can's field drags the can after the magnet
items.why: A moving magnet makes the swirls, the swirls make a field of their own, and that field acts on the magnet. The can is dragged along.

items.p: A magnet sticks firmly to the base of a pan but not to the sides. Will the pan heat on an induction stove?
opts: Probably yes, because the base touches the stove and is magnetic
No, because the sides are not magnetic
No, because pans need to stick everywhere
items.why: The stove heats the part of the pan that sits on it. A magnetic base heats well.

items.p: A steel spoon that does not stick at its smooth bowl might stick slightly at its bent neck.
items.why: True for some stainless steels. Bending changes how the atoms are packed, and some tiny magnets can then line up.

items.p: A tin can is steel with a very thin coat of tin on it. A magnet sticks to the can. Why?
opts: The magnet feels the steel under the thin coat of tin
items.why: Tin is not magnetic, but the coat is very thin and the steel is what the magnet feels. A name for a thing may describe only its outside.

items.p: Sort each of these by what a very strong lab magnet does to it: pulls strongly, pulls extremely weakly, or pushes extremely weakly.
items.why: Iron and nickel are ferromagnetic. Aluminium and oxygen are paramagnetic. Water and copper are diamagnetic.

items.p: A kabadiwala says, 'I know aluminium by its weight and its dull ring, and I do not need a magnet.' Is that a good way to tell aluminium from steel? Give a reason.
items.a: Yes, it can be a good way. Aluminium is lighter than steel for the same size, and rings differently. A magnet only shows that steel is there, and says little about aluminium. A good sorter uses several clues.
items.why: A strong answer says that more than one clue helps, and that the magnet is good at one job only.

items.p: Two friends watch a magnet swing over an aluminium plate and stop quickly. They argue about what to call aluminium.

views.says: Aluminium is non-magnetic. A fridge magnet does not stick to it.
Aluminium is magnetic in a way. A moving magnet is slowed by it, so it does respond.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give one piece of evidence. Then say what each friend is right about.
items.a: Both can be right. The first friend is right that a still magnet does not hold aluminium. The second friend is right that a moving magnet is slowed by it. A strong answer says the word 'magnetic' needs a test: still or moving.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the swinging magnet and from the still magnet, and sees what each friend gets right.

items.p: Draw a conveyor belt with four stations in a good order: a magnet, a spinning magnet drum, an air blower and hands. Label what each station takes out.
items.a: A belt starting with a heap. The magnet comes first and takes out steel. Then the drum throws off aluminium and other non-ferrous metals. The blower lifts light paper. Hands pick the rest.
items.why: Steel must come out before the drum, so it does not stick to it.
items.art: A blank conveyor belt drawn from the side.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a recycling line. Label the three parts: the steel lifter, the spinning drum and the bin of aluminium.
labels: Magnets spinning inside the belt roller
Bin at the end of the belt that cans leap into
items.art: A drawing of a conveyor belt with a big magnet above it, a spinning drum at its end and a bin in front of the drum.
a: Big magnet over the belt: steel lifter
Magnets spinning inside the belt roller: spinning drum
Bin at the end of the belt that cans leap into: bin of aluminium
items.why: The big magnet lifts steel. The drum makes swirls in the aluminium, which throws the cans forward into their bin.

items.p: Why is the oxygen in the air called paramagnetic?
opts: It is pulled extremely weakly by a very strong magnet
It sticks to a fridge magnet
items.why: Oxygen is attracted extremely weakly. Liquid oxygen, which is very cold, clings between the poles of a strong magnet.

items.p: Match each device to the job it does.
pairs: Eddy current brake
slows a roller coaster car without touching it
Induction stove
heats a pan with a magnetic base
Metal detector
finds a buried coin that a magnet does not attract
Magnetic separator
lifts steel cans out of mixed waste
items.why: Each device uses a magnet in a different way. A strong answer can say which ones use attraction and which use eddy currents.

items.p: A metal detector finds a gold ring because the ring makes ____ currents in the detector's changing magnetic field.
items.why: The detector senses the eddy currents. Gold is not attracted by a still magnet, but it carries electricity.

items.p: Three of these are good conductors of electricity. Which one is an insulator?
items.why: Plastic does not carry electricity. Copper, silver and aluminium carry it well.

items.p: A cold-drink can follows a fast magnet, but a steel can sticks even to a still magnet. How are the two pushes or pulls different?
items.a: The steel can is attracted by a still magnet because iron has lined-up tiny magnets. The aluminium can is dragged only while the magnet moves, because swirling currents push against it.
items.why: A strong answer names one cause for each: tiny magnets in the steel, and swirling currents in the aluminium.

worksheets.title: What Does a Magnet Really Tell Us? (challenge)

items.p: A shop says, 'This pan is magnetic, so it is stainless steel.' What is wrong with this?
opts: Plain steel is magnetic too, so a magnet cannot show it is stainless
Magnetic pans are made of aluminium
items.why: Plain steel also sticks to a magnet. Stainless steel is a family. Some kinds stick and some do not. A magnet cannot name the steel.

items.p: A magnet falls slowly down a thick copper pipe. What would make the fall even slower?
opts: A pipe with a thicker wall made of copper
A pipe with slits cut along it
items.why: More copper means more room for swirls, so a stronger push up. Slits break the swirls, and plastic and wood have none.

items.p: An induction stove would heat an aluminium pan just as well as a pan with a thick magnetic steel base.
items.why: False. An aluminium pan is not magnetic and carries electricity so well that it heats very little. A pan with a magnetic steel base heats much better.

items.p: A magnet is held still above a copper plate and nothing happens. Then it is moved quickly and is dragged. What does this tell us about the effect?
opts: It needs the magnet to be moving
It needs the plate to be magnetic
It needs the plate to be hot
It only happens in the dark
items.why: The swirls form only while the magnetic field around the plate is changing. A still magnet makes no change.

items.p: Common stainless steel has nickel mixed in. This changes how the iron atoms are packed, so a magnet ____ sticks to it.
items.why: The packing keeps the tiny magnets of the iron atoms from lining up, so the steel is almost not attracted.

items.p: Why is it better to say 'a still magnet does not attract aluminium' than to say 'aluminium is not magnetic'?
items.a: The second sentence suggests aluminium never answers a magnet. But a moving magnet does push on it, and a very strong magnet pulls it extremely weakly. The first sentence says exactly what we tested.
items.why: A strong answer says that a plain statement should match the test that was done.

items.p: Match each tool or device to the main idea it uses.
pairs: A scrapyard crane magnet
a magnet attracts iron and steel
A spinning-drum separator
a moving magnet makes eddy currents in aluminium
An induction stove
a changing magnetic field heats a magnetic steel pan
A metal detector
a changing field makes eddy currents in any metal that conducts
items.why: Some of these use attraction and some use eddy currents. A strong answer can say which is which.

items.p: A rusty nail still sticks to a magnet, but the brown flakes mostly do not. What is the best explanation?
opts: The nail still has an iron core, and the rust is only weakly magnetic
items.why: A magnet feels iron that is still iron. The rust is iron joined with oxygen and water, which is only weakly magnetic.

items.p: A city plans to build a centre with machines to sort all its waste. Waste pickers say they should be part of the plan.

views.says: A centre sorts faster and the work is safer than picking by hand.
Pickers know hundreds of materials by touch and sound, and the centre needs them to sort what machines cannot.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with? Give a reason from the unit. Then say how both might work together.
items.a: Either can be argued, and both are partly right. A centre sorts steel and aluminium quickly, but hands and eyes still do much of the sorting. A strong answer says how both can work together, for example by employing the pickers in the centre.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that machines are good at some steps and people at others.

items.p: A magnet that is moving makes electricity in a nearby piece of metal even if the metal is not magnetic.
items.why: True. Faraday found in 1831 that a moving magnet makes electric currents in a conductor. The metal does not have to be magnetic.

items.p: A magnet does not stick to a coin. Someone says this proves the coin is real silver. What does the test truly show?
opts: The coin is not made of iron, nickel or cobalt on the surface, but it could be many things
The coin has no metal in it
items.why: Many metals ignore a still magnet. A magnet that does not stick rules out only a few.

items.p: A material can answer a still magnet with nothing and a moving magnet with a push. Does this mean that a material has no fixed nature? Argue either side.
items.a: One side: the material's atoms have a fixed structure, and the two answers both come from it, so its nature is fixed. Other side: what we call its nature is how it answers our tests, and different tests give different answers, so a label depends on the test.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason for the side it chooses and says what the other side would say.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a magnet falling through a copper pipe. Label the magnet, the swirls of current and the upward push.
labels: Curved arrows in the pipe wall
Arrow pointing up on the magnet
items.art: A drawing of a copper pipe seen from the side with a magnet inside, curved arrows in the pipe wall and an arrow pointing up.
a: Curved arrows in the pipe wall: swirls of current
Arrow pointing up on the magnet: upward push
items.why: The magnet makes swirls in the pipe. The swirls make a field that pushes up against the falling magnet.

items.p: In a recycling centre, which step uses an eddy current separator?
opts: Throwing aluminium cans off the belt
Lifting steel cans off the belt
items.why: The spinning drum makes eddy currents in aluminium and other non-ferrous metals, and these push the pieces forward. The magnet lifts steel. The blower lifts paper.

items.p: On Mars, magnets on rovers have collected dust, which shows that some of the dust has magnetic iron minerals in it.
items.why: True. Magnets on Mars landers and rovers collected dark magnetic dust. The red colour of Mars is from iron joined with oxygen.

items.p: Plastic, wood and glass do not drag a moving magnet because they are ____, which do not carry electricity.
items.why: No electricity can flow in a swirl, so no field is made to push back.

items.p: Draw your kitchen map in three zones: sticks firmly, sticks weakly, does not stick. Put at least two things in each zone, and write the name of one thing that surprised you.
items.a: Three labelled zones. A typical map has a steel pan base and a tawa under 'sticks firmly', a tumbler rim under 'sticks weakly', and an aluminium kadai, a brass lamp and a glass jar under 'does not stick'.
items.why: A strong map has three zones with examples, and a note about a surprise.
items.art: A blank sheet with three empty boxes.

items.p: A magnet-based tester says a pan 'will not work' on an induction stove. When might the tester be wrong, and what should a shopper do?
items.a: The magnet may not stick to some special pans that have been made for induction in a different way, or may stick to the sides but not the base. A shopper should read the maker's label as well.
items.why: A strong answer says that the tester is a rough guide and the label gives the final word.

quiz.p: Which materials does a still magnet strongly attract?
quiz.why: Only iron, nickel, cobalt and some mixtures are attracted strongly. Many other metals ignore a still magnet.

quiz.p: Which of these is extremely weakly pushed away by a very strong magnet?
quiz.why: Water is diamagnetic, so it is pushed away extremely weakly. Iron, nickel and cobalt are pulled strongly.

quiz.p: A magnet sticks to the rim of a steel tumbler, but hardly to its wall. What is the best explanation?
opts: Rolling the rim may have changed the steel inside, so more tiny magnets line up
The rim is made of a different metal
The magnet is stronger at the rim
quiz.why: Bending and rolling can change how atoms are packed in some stainless steels.

quiz.p: A fast-moving magnet makes an aluminium can roll. What is the main reason?
opts: It makes swirling electric currents in the can
The can becomes a magnet like iron
The magnet sticks to the can
quiz.why: The swirls make a magnetic field that drags the can. A still magnet does nothing.

quiz.p: What name do we give the swirling currents a moving magnet makes in metal?
quiz.why: An eddy is a small whirl, like a river's swirl behind a rock.

quiz.p: Which of these will drag a moving magnet the most?
quiz.why: Copper carries electricity very well, so strong swirls form in it. The others are insulators.

quiz.p: A magnet dropped through a plastic pipe falls fast. Dropped through a copper pipe of the same size, it falls slowly. Why?
opts: Swirling currents in the copper push up against the falling magnet
quiz.why: Plastic makes no swirls. Copper makes them, and they push against the movement.

quiz.p: A recycling centre first lifts steel off the belt with a magnet. Why?
opts: So the steel does not stick to the spinning drum that throws off aluminium
quiz.why: A drum of magnets would hold the steel cans instead of letting them pass.

quiz.p: Which machine throws aluminium cans off a conveyor belt?
opts: A big magnet over the belt
quiz.why: A spinning magnetic drum makes eddy currents in the aluminium that push the cans forward.

quiz.p: A pan works on an induction stove. What is likely to be true of its base?
opts: A magnet sticks firmly to it
quiz.why: A magnetic steel base heats well in the stove's changing field.

quiz.p: Why does an aluminium pan heat poorly on an induction stove?
opts: It is not magnetic and carries electricity so well that it heats very little
quiz.why: A magnetic steel base heats strongly. Aluminium heats very little.

quiz.p: A magnet does not stick to a ring. What can you truly say?
opts: The ring is not made of iron, nickel or cobalt on the surface, but it could be many other things
quiz.why: Many metals ignore a still magnet, including gold, silver, copper, brass and aluminium.

quiz.p: A metal detector finds a brass key in the ground. Brass is not attracted by a still magnet. How can the detector find it?
opts: It senses the eddy currents the key makes
quiz.why: The detector's changing field makes eddy currents in any conducting metal.

quiz.p: A rusty nail sticks to a magnet. What is the best reason?
opts: The nail still has an iron core under the rust
quiz.why: The rust itself is only weakly magnetic, but the iron under it is.

opts: A still magnet does not attract aluminium, but a moving magnet pushes on it
Aluminium is not affected by magnets
quiz.why: The best sentence says what the test was. A still magnet and a moving magnet give different answers.

applications: Recycling centres lift steel with magnets and throw aluminium cans off belts with eddy current separators.
Induction stoves heat pans with a base of magnetic steel and no flame.
Metal detectors at airports, temples and shops find any metal that carries electricity.
Roller coasters and some trains slow down with eddy current brakes, using strong magnets and metal fins that never touch.
Scrap dealers and kabadiwalas test metal by sound, weight, colour and, sometimes, a magnet.
Mining companies use big magnets to take iron minerals out of crushed rock.
Food factories pass flour and spices over magnets to catch tiny pieces of iron before packing.
Engineers choose stainless steel for sinks, tumblers and tanks, and use a magnet to check which kind it is.
Electricity meters in some homes use a spinning aluminium disc, slowed by a magnet, to count units.
Archaeologists use metal detectors and magnetometers to find buried metal and old fires without digging.
Spacecraft scientists put magnets on rovers to collect dust and study the rocks of other planets.
Jewellers use many tests, not just a magnet, because a magnet cannot say whether a ring is gold.

open_questions.q: Can we make a very strong magnet from common, cheap elements?
open_questions.why_open: The strongest magnets use rare earth metals, which are hard to dig out and separate. Scientists are searching for new materials that do not need them.

open_questions.q: Why do iron, nickel and cobalt line up their tiny magnets, when almost every other element does not?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics gives good explanations. Predicting exactly which new mixtures will be strong magnets is still hard.

open_questions.q: How can a machine tell the many kinds of plastic apart, as it tells steel and aluminium apart?
open_questions.why_open: Plastics look alike and are not magnetic. Cameras and light sensors help, but sorting every kind well and cheaply is still being worked on.

open_questions.q: How and when did Mars lose its magnetic field, and what did that do to its air?
open_questions.why_open: Rocks on Mars hold a record of an old field. Scientists argue about when it faded and how much that mattered.

open_questions.q: Is there a limit to how many times a metal can be recycled?
open_questions.why_open: Aluminium and steel can be melted again and again, but small amounts of other metals build up. Where this stops is a question for engineers.

open_questions.q: Can a material push a magnet away perfectly at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Superconductors push magnets away perfectly, but only when very cold. Finding one that works at room temperature is one of the biggest open questions in materials science.
