maths.problem: A magnet swinging over a wooden board makes 24 swings before it stops. Over an aluminium plate it makes 4 swings. How many times as many swings does it make over wood?
maths.explain: 24 divided by 4 is 6. So the magnet makes 6 times as many swings over wood. Check: 4 times 6 is 24.
maths.context: In the Pendulum That Stops experiment, you count the swings of a magnet over different plates.
maths.why_maths: A ratio like '6 times as many' tells you how much a plate slows the magnet. It is easier to compare than two separate numbers.

maths.problem: Five fast swishes made an aluminium can roll 14, 18, 12, 16 and 15 centimetres. What is the middle value, and why is it a good number to report?
maths.answer: The middle value is 15 centimetres. It is a good number because one odd roll does not change it much.
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18. The middle one is 15. If one of the rolls had been 40 instead, the middle value would be 15 or 16, which is hardly any change, while the biggest would jump to 40.
maths.context: In the Can That Follows experiment, you swish a magnet past an aluminium can five times and measure how far it rolls.
maths.why_maths: The middle value of several tries is steadier than any one try. It stops a single fluke from fooling you.

maths.problem: In a recycling centre, a conveyor belt is 24 metres long and moves 2 metres every second. How many seconds does a can take to ride from one end to the other?
maths.explain: 24 metres divided by 2 metres a second is 12 seconds. Check: 12 seconds times 2 metres is 24 metres.
maths.context: In the Plan a Sorting Line activity, you plan the stations along a conveyor belt.
maths.why_maths: Engineers use division to find how long a can spends under each machine. The time tells them how strong the magnet must be.

maths.problem: About 60 aluminium cans weigh 1 kilogram. A made-up price for aluminium is 90 rupees a kilogram. A waste picker has 180 cans. How much money are they worth?
maths.explain: 180 divided by 60 is 3, so the cans weigh about 3 kilograms. 3 times 90 is 270 rupees. The price here is made up, and real prices change from day to day.
maths.context: In the Ask a Kabadiwala or Waste Picker activity, you find out that sorters are paid by weight.
maths.why_maths: Sorters are paid by weight, so they need to work out kilograms from a count of cans. Two steps of division and multiplication give the money.

maths.problem: In the Kitchen Metal Map, 7 of 20 things stuck firmly, 3 stuck weakly and 10 did not stick. What fraction stuck firmly, and what percentage is that?
maths.explain: 7 out of 20 is the fraction. To turn it into a percentage, multiply the top and bottom by 5 to make hundredths. 7 times 5 is 35, and 20 times 5 is 100. So it is 35 hundredths, or 35 percent.
maths.context: In the Kitchen Metal Map project, you test twenty kitchen things with a magnet and make a poster.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare the kitchen with a friend's kitchen, even when you tested a different number of things.

maths.problem: Three friends swished a magnet past a can and measured the roll. They got 15 cm, 16 cm and 2 cm. Which result is odd, and what could explain it? What middle value would you report?
maths.answer: The 2 centimetre roll is odd. The middle value is 15 centimetres.
maths.explain: In order, the numbers are 2, 15, 16. The middle is 15. The 2 is far from the others. The swish might have been slow, or the magnet may have been further from the can. A good scientist repeats that try before throwing it away.
maths.context: In the Can That Follows experiment, you compare your rolls with those of other people.
maths.why_maths: Spotting an odd result and asking why is part of good science. It tells you what to check in the way you did the test.

maths.problem: A magnet over a wooden board makes 15 swings in 30 seconds. How long does one swing take, and how many swings would it make in one minute?
maths.answer: One swing takes 2 seconds, and it would make 30 swings in a minute.
maths.explain: 30 seconds divided by 15 swings is 2 seconds a swing. A minute is 60 seconds, and 60 divided by 2 is 30 swings. Check: 15 swings in 30 seconds is 30 swings in 60 seconds.
maths.context: In the Pendulum That Stops experiment, you count the swings of a magnet on a thread.
maths.why_maths: The time of one swing stays almost the same as the swings get smaller. Knowing it lets you count swings by watching a clock.

maths.problem: The spinning drum in a recycling centre turns 600 times in a minute. How many times does it turn in one second, and how many times in five seconds?
maths.answer: 10 times in a second, and 50 times in five seconds.
maths.explain: A minute is 60 seconds. 600 divided by 60 is 10 turns a second. In 5 seconds, 5 times 10 is 50 turns.
maths.context: In the Plan a Sorting Line activity, the spinning magnet drum throws aluminium cans off the belt.
maths.why_maths: A fast-changing magnetic field is what makes the strong swirls. Knowing the turns each second tells you how fast the field changes.

roots.context: In this unit you mapped where a magnet sticks on kitchen steel, made an aluminium can follow a magnet, and swung a magnet over four plates. Now we ask what these tests tell us about materials, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: A still magnet ignores an aluminium can. A magnet swished past it makes the can roll. So what a material does near a magnet depends on what the magnet is doing, as well as on the material.
deep_truth.habit: We say a material is magnetic or is not magnetic, as if that were a fixed label like its colour. But the label only reports how the material answered one test, with a still magnet.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Can That Follows, the aluminium can ignored a still magnet and followed a fast one. In the Pendulum That Stops, the aluminium plate stopped the magnet and the wooden board did not.

three.who_am_i: A person can sit quietly when nothing moves, and answer strongly when something rushes at them. The same person gives two different answers.
three.what_is_life: A bacterium senses whether the food around her is getting richer or poorer, not only how much there is. Many living beings notice change more than stillness.
three.what_is_this_world: A still magnet and a moving magnet are the same magnet. What a thing does depends on what is happening around it.

roots.thread: A magnet and a lump of aluminium can sit side by side and nothing happens. Move the magnet, and electricity swirls in the aluminium. The swirls were not there before, yet nothing was added from outside. The aluminium was able to do this all along. It needed a change to show it. So one label, such as 'not magnetic', does not describe a material fully. A material can answer in several ways, and each test shows only one of them.

teachings.link: The words magnetic and non-magnetic are made by people, for the answer to one test. They are useful, but they do not say everything about the material.

science.text: A moving magnet makes eddy currents in any conductor, and these push against the movement. Faraday found induction in 1831 and Lenz stated the rule in 1834.
Whether labels such as magnetic and non-magnetic belong to the material or to the test is a question about words, and thinkers differ.

other_view.view: Ferromagnetic, paramagnetic and diamagnetic are real, fixed properties of the electrons and atoms in a material. The moving-magnet push is a separate effect that belongs to electricity. To say labels are made by us hides the fact that the atoms have a definite structure.

practice.title: A hand in the water

how_we_found_out.story: In 1824, the French scientist Francois Arago spun a copper disc under a compass needle. The needle turned, though copper is not magnetic and nothing touched it. People called it magnetism of rotation, and many thought that spinning made copper magnetic. In 1831, Michael Faraday showed that a moving magnet makes electric currents in a nearby conductor. Heinrich Lenz showed in 1834 that these currents push against the movement that makes them. In 1855, Leon Foucault found that a copper disc spun between the poles of a strong magnet gets hot. The swirling currents have been called eddy currents ever since. The same swirls are used in induction stoves, metal detectors and recycling centres.
how_we_found_out.who: Francois Arago, Michael Faraday, Heinrich Lenz and Leon Foucault
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought spinning made copper magnetic, in the way iron is magnetic, and called it magnetism of rotation. Faraday's work showed that the needle was turned by the swirling currents that the moving copper makes in the needle's magnetic field.
